subject: Version Control Systems

assessmentTargets.concept: Identify the three areas of a Git workflow: working directory, staging area, and repository
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one you have is git add. So this is, if you remember in your git workflow, I told you we have three areas. Working directory, stagi
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to list the three areas and briefly describe their purpose.

assessmentTargets.concept: Use `git add .` to stage all modified files in the working directory
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: you can simply write git add space dot, that means all the changes that you have done in your project will be saved.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Provide a scenario and require the student to write the correct git add command.

assessmentTargets.concept: Explain how `git commit -m "message"` creates a repository snapshot and records a descriptive message
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Git commit will save the changes of your particular file into the repository... you have to give a message.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Explanation of git commit and its message
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to describe what happens when a commit is made and why a message is important.

assessmentTargets.concept: Use `git diff` to compare the current working files against the previous commit
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: git diff will compare the changes of your current file with the previous version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Present two file states and ask the student to predict the output of git diff.

assessmentTargets.concept: Differentiate between `git reset` (reverts staged changes) and `git restore` (reverts working‑tree changes)
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: When you type git reset. All the changes will be reverted back.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Give a situation where a student has staged but not committed changes and ask which command to use and why.

reserveTargets.concept: Initialize a new Git repository with `git init`
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: You have to type git space init. ... this particular folder ... is converted into a git repository.
reserveTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to write the command that creates a .git folder.

reserveTargets.concept: Interpret the output of `git status` to determine staged vs unstaged files
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: git status ... tells you there is one file called as a.ext in which you did not save anything.
reserveTargets.instruction: Provide a sample git status output and ask the learner to identify which files are staged.

Initialize a new Git repository with `git init`
